title: Sudden left lower abdominal pain with vomiting

source.citation: Carius BM, Houston EJ, Griffith SP. A Case Report of Massive Intraperitoneal Hemorrhage from Rare Cornual Pregnancy. Clin Pract Cases Emerg Med. 2022;6(1):41-44.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Left lower abdominal pain and vomiting for 20 minutes
presentation.hpi: Twenty minutes of left-sided lower abdominal pain with four episodes of non-bloody vomiting; no vaginal bleeding. Both of her previous ectopic pregnancies were treated with intramuscular methotrexate: one about six months ago, and one declared resolved a month ago after the beta-hCG fell from over 16,000 to 1700 mIU/mL (measured two weeks before arrival).
pmh: Two previous ectopic pregnancies, both treated with methotrexate

imaging.finding: Free fluid in the abdomen; thickened endometrium with an endometrial mass

diagnosis.primary: Ruptured left cornual (interstitial) ectopic pregnancy with about 2 L of intraperitoneal hemorrhage

management: 1 L saline bolus: transient rise in blood pressure to 108/58 mm Hg
Two units of packed red cells en route to the operating room
Cornual wedge resection and unilateral salpingectomy
outcome: Uneventful recovery; discharged on postoperative day three.
teachingPoints: An ectopic pregnancy declared resolved after methotrexate can still rupture; a falling beta-hCG does not exclude it.
Interstitial (cornual) pregnancies tend to rupture later and bleed more because of the myometrial blood supply, and can look intrauterine on ultrasound.
Hypotension with a normal heart rate does not exclude hemorrhagic shock; free fluid on bedside ultrasound needs emergency gynecological review.

questions.q: She has just fainted. What is the most useful immediate investigation?
questions.extra: After 1 L of saline her BP rose transiently to 108/58 mm Hg; first hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL. Standing up to give a urine sample, she becomes pale and faints for under a minute: BP now 68/38 mm Hg, HR 108/min.
options: Urine pregnancy test before anything else
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.explanation: Bedside ultrasound finds free intraperitoneal fluid within minutes and must not wait for a urine test or CT in an unstable patient; here it showed free fluid and an endometrial mass. The first hemoglobin is often normal in acute hemorrhage, because dilution takes time.

questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.extra: Bedside ultrasound: free fluid in the abdomen; thickened endometrium with an endometrial mass. Repeat hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL.
questions.explanation: Two previous ectopics treated medically, a beta-hCG still at 1700 mIU/mL two weeks ago, hypotension, free fluid and a falling hemoglobin mean a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until surgery proves otherwise. At operation it was a ruptured left cornual (interstitial) ectopic with about 2 L of blood in the abdomen.

A ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemodynamic instability needs emergency surgery and blood products (NICE NG126); methotrexate and expectant management are only for stable, unruptured cases. She received two units of red cells on the way to theatre and had a cornual wedge resection with salpingectomy.

evidence.quote: A 34-year-old gravida four, para two female with history of two ectopic pregnancies
arrived at the ED complaining of 20 minutes of left-sided lower abdominal pain with four episodes of non-bloody emesis
She denied other symptoms, including vaginal bleeding.
approximately six months prior to arrival at the ED, resolved with intramuscular methotrexate
deemed resolved after intramuscular methotrexate one month prior to arrival
After initial quantitative beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (βhCG) of over 16,000 milli-international units per milliliter (mIU/mL)
her levels fell to 1700 mIU/mL two weeks prior to arrival
Triage vital signs were significant for blood pressure (BP) of 86/51 millimeters mercury (mm Hg)
but were otherwise within normal limits, including a heart rate (HR) of 85 beats per minutes (bpm)
Physical examination revealed voluntary guarding of the abdomen and only moderate tenderness of the left lower quadrant.
initial complete blood count (CBC) found stable hemoglobin and hematocrit of 12.0 grams/deciliter (g/dL)
repeat hemoglobin and hematocrit revealed a dramatic decline to 6.2 g/dL and 20.1%
Point-of-care US revealed free fluid in the abdomen as well as a thickened endometrium with an endometrial mass
The surgeons found approximately two liters of intraperitoneal blood and diagnosed a ruptured, left cornual ectopic pregnancy
A one-liter saline intravenous bolus provided transient BP improvement to 108/58 mm Hg
Two units of packed red blood cells were administered en route to the operating room.
A cornual wedge resection and a unilateral salpingectomy were performed.
The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day three.
